content: The evidence profile compares the effectiveness of trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (TF-CBT) with and without the inclusion of a trauma narrative in children who have experienced sexual maltreatment. The following are the detailed findings: 1. Re-experiencing Symptoms: The re-experiencing subscale of the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children (K-SADS-E) was used to assess outcomes. The possible range of scores was not provided. The quality of evidence was rated as very low due to imprecise effect estimates and small sample sizes (<300 participants). 2. Avoidance Symptoms: The avoidance subscale of the K-SADS-E was used to measure outcomes. Again, the possible range of scores was not provided. The evidence quality was rated as very low for similar reasons as above. 3. Hypervigilance Symptoms: The hypervigilance subscale of the K-SADS-E was used to evaluate outcomes. The possible range of scores was not provided. The evidence quality was rated as very low. 4. Depression Symptoms: Depression was assessed using the Children’s Depression Inventory (CDI), a 27-item scale with a total possible score range of 0–54. A score of 19 or higher indicates severe depression. The evidence quality was rated as very low due to imprecise estimates and small sample sizes. 5. Anxiety Symptoms: Anxiety was measured using the Multidimensional Anxiety Scale for Children (MASC), a 39-item scale with a score range of 0–117. T-scores above 70 indicate clinical anxiety. The evidence quality was rated as very low. 6. Internalizing Symptoms: Internalizing symptoms were assessed using the internalizing subscale of the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL-Int). T-scores range from 0–100, with scores below 60 considered normal, 60–63 as borderline, and above 63 in the clinical range. The evidence quality was rated as very low. 7. Externalizing Symptoms: Externalizing symptoms were measured using the externalizing subscale of the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL-Ext). The scoring system is the same as for internalizing symptoms. The evidence quality was rated as very low. 8. Follow-up at 6 Months: Outcomes at six months post-treatment were assessed for PTSD symptoms (re-experiencing, avoidance, and hypervigilance), depression, anxiety, and behavioral symptoms. The quality of evidence remained very low across all measures due to small sample sizes and imprecise estimates. 9. Follow-up at 12 Months: Similar outcomes were assessed at 12 months post-treatment, including PTSD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and behavioral symptoms. The evidence quality was consistently rated as very low. 10. Comparison of 16-Session TF-CBT with and without Trauma Narrative: The findings for the 16-session intervention mirrored those of the 8-session intervention, with very low-quality evidence across all outcomes. Depression, anxiety, and behavioral symptoms were assessed using the same tools (CDI, MASC, CBCL-Int, and CBCL-Ext). 11. Comparison of TF-CBT to Non-CBT Interventions: When comparing TF-CBT to non-CBT interventions, the evidence quality was rated as low to very low. PTSD symptoms were assessed using the K-SADS-E and the Trauma Symptom Checklist for Children (TSC-C). The TSC-C is a 10-item scale with a score range of 0–30. Limitations of the Evidence: The sample sizes in the studies were consistently small (<300 participants), leading to imprecise effect estimates. Many outcomes were assessed using endpoint or follow-up data only, with no baseline data available for comparison. There were serious concerns about the risk of bias in the included studies. GRADE Evidence Ratings: High Quality: Very confident that the true effect is close to the estimated effect. Moderate Quality: Moderately confident; the true effect is likely close to the estimate but may differ substantially. Low Quality: Limited confidence; the true effect may differ substantially from the estimate. Very Low Quality: Very little confidence; the true effect is likely substantially different from the estimate. In summary, the evidence supporting the use of TF-CBT with or without a trauma narrative for children who have experienced sexual maltreatment is of very low quality. This highlights the need for further research with larger sample sizes and more rigorous study designs to provide more reliable conclusions.
